claim_text: Global Interpreter Lock (GIL).
evidence_span: Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)

claim_text: » What is the GIL? » A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) that protects access to Python objects in CPython (the default Python implementation). » Ensures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. » Why does it exist? » Simplifies memory management in CPython, especially with reference counting for garbage collection. » Avoids race conditions and ensures thread safety in single-threaded contexts. » Implications for Multithreading » Limits true parallelism in CPU-bound tasks, as only one thread can execute Python code at any moment. » I/O-bound tasks can still benefit from multithreading since the GIL is released during I/O operations (e.g., file I/O, network requests).

claim_text: » What is the GIL? » A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) that protects access to Python objects in CPython (the default Python implementation). » Ensures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. » Why does it exist? » Simplifies memory management in CPython, especially with reference counting for garbage collection. » Avoids race conditions and ensures thread safety in single-threaded contexts. » Implications for Multithreading » Limits true parallelism in CPU-bound tasks, as only one thread can execute Python code at any moment. » I/O-bound tasks can still benefit from multithreading since the GIL is released during I/O operations (e.g., file I/O, network requests).

claim_text: Your processing should therefore be idempotent (e.g. upsert by an event id instead of count += 1).

Your processing should therefore be *idempotent* (e.g. upsert by an event id instead of `count += 1`).

claim_text: Bridge to the main lab: pandas runs most operations on one core.
evidence_span: **Bridge to the main lab:** pandas runs most operations on one core. Polars (Rust) and DuckDB (C++) run their work *outside* the GIL on all cores – no multiprocessing tricks needed. Spark goes one step further: many processes on **many machines**.
